justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish near-term bias with gradual upward drift over time. For the one-day estimate, I anchored close to what would have been the prevailing market level, assuming no major overnight catalysts and typical mean-reversion behavior within a narrow intraday range. The one-week estimate steps slightly higher, reflecting a baseline assumption that equity markets tend to drift upward over short horizons in the absence of negative shocks, consistent with a modest risk-on environment. The one-month estimate continues that gentle upward trajectory, incorporating a small equity risk premium over the period while acknowledging that longer horizons allow more time for either positive momentum or fundamental revaluation to accumulate.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds with time. At the one-day horizon, the interval is relatively tight because most of the price-setting information for the next session is already partially embedded in current prices, and large gaps are statistically uncommon on any given day. By one week, macro data releases, Fed communications, and geopolitical developments can materially shift sentiment, so the interval widens to capture that additional noise. At one month, the range becomes substantially wider because the cumulative effect of earnings surprises, inflation prints, central bank decisions, and global risk appetite shifts can push prices well beyond what short-term drift would suggest.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals include a sudden and unexpected shift in Federal Reserve policy language, a significant geopolitical escalation affecting energy markets or global supply chains, or a major earnings disappointment from systemically important companies. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected economic data release or a resolution of an ongoing geopolitical tension could generate a sharp rally beyond the upper bound. These tail events are precisely why the stated 90% confidence intervals, while wide, still exclude roughly one in ten plausible outcomes, and real-world distributions tend to have fatter tails than normal assumptions imply.

It is also worth noting that my estimates are subject to model uncertainty itself. I do not have access to real-time market data, options-implied volatility surfaces, or order flow information that professional forecasters would typically incorporate. This means my confidence intervals may be miscalibrated in either direction, and any significant structural break in market conditions, such as a liquidity crisis or a sudden shift in correlations, could render even these wide bands insufficient.
